frase_gancho.texto: A young man made of stucco, with three flowers in his hairstyle, found beside Pakal.

puente_narrativo.texto: From the father’s tomb we move on to the son’s stone. Look for a large limestone panel where the same king appears twice, as a child and as an adult, on either side of a sacred cross.

guion_corto.texto: This head is modeled in stucco, a mixture of lime, powdered limestone, and water that was worked like clay and hardened like stone. It was found in [Pakal’s tomb](mna_s09_cripta_pakal), in Palenque, beneath the sarcophagus. It portrays a young man with a sharp face, almond-shaped eyes, and full lips. Notice the profile: the nose continues almost straight up to the forehead, the result of a cranial modification that was achieved from infancy. The hair is divided into locks, and on the front it bears three flower buds, a symbol tied to maize and to vegetation. It is believed to have been cut off on purpose from a complete sculpture and placed as an offering. No one knows for certain whom it represents.

guion_largo.texto:
This head has something that places it among the most delicate portraits of Maya art: serenity. And at the same time, something unsettling: it is cut off. It is not a bust, but what remains of a complete figure, whose head was removed.

To understand it, we have to imagine what Palenque was like. Its temples and palaces were not the color of the stone you see today in photographs. They were covered in stucco, modeled and painted in red, blue, and yellow, with life-size figures of gods and kings. The sculptors of Palenque were famous for their stucco: soft, fluid, and realistic. This head, in fact, belonged to one of those figures.

Why cut it off? The archaeologists who found it thought it was done on purpose. It is believed that, when the king died, an image was “killed” so that it would accompany him, just as people close to him or objects he had used were buried. Remember San Lorenzo, in the Gulf Hall, where the Olmec monuments were mutilated and buried: in Mesoamerica, an image was something alive, and destroying it was also a way of offering it.

Imagine the moment of the discovery. When Ruz lifted the floor slabs of the crypt, beneath the enormous sarcophagus, he found a deposit of ceramic vessels and, among them, two stucco heads. Above them weighed several tons of stone and more than one thousand two hundred years. Someone had placed those heads with care, like someone leaving a gift at the foot of a bed.

Now notice the profile. The forehead slopes back in an almost continuous line with the nose. It is not a natural feature: it was achieved from babyhood, by binding the head between small boards, the custom you saw in the introductory hall and in the faces of [Offering 4](mna_s08_ofrenda4_laventa). Some think that this profile recalled the shape of an ear of tender maize, and that this is why it was a symbol of beauty and nobility. [Pakal](mna_s09_mascara_pakal), in his jade mask, has the same profile.

The three buds in the hairstyle speak too. Flowers, for the Maya, were synonymous with beauty, with the sacred, and with the sprouting of maize. That there are three, on the forehead, at the side, and at the back, suggests a crown of vegetation encircling the head. It has been proposed that this is the young Maize God (Corn God), or a prince who identifies with him. There is no way to know for certain.

One last curiosity about this tomb: from it a stone tube rises to the temple, passing through the staircase. It is believed to have served so that the king’s spirit could keep communicating with the world above. A tomb with a direct line to the living.

So look again at this young man: his almond-shaped eyes, his half-open mouth. However much it may be a “decapitated” piece, nothing in his face seems sad. He seems to be waiting. When you see it in the display case, stand to one side to view the profile: it is the best way to understand the ideal of beauty of the Maya nobility.

texto: Notice the profile: how does the nose continue up to the forehead?
Find the three flower buds in the hairstyle
Observe the locks of hair: how are they cut?

texto.Discovery: 1952, by Alberto Ruz Lhuillier, beneath the sarcophagus of Pakal, in the burial chamber of the Temple of the Inscriptions

texto.pregunta: Myth: The Maya made their sculptures only in stone and without color.
texto.respuesta: Reality: Many were modeled in stucco and painted in bright colors; over the centuries, the paint was lost.
